title: Book 1 — Clio, Chapter 184
paragraphs: The queen who ruled after her, named Nitocris, was far wiser. She left behind monuments I will describe. She also saw that the Median empire was growing powerful and restless, having already captured Nineveh among other cities. She took every possible precaution against them. First, she diverted the river Euphrates, which had previously run straight through the center of the city. By digging channels upstream, she made it wind so much that it passed one particular Assyrian village three times. (The village is called Ardericca, and anyone sailing down the Euphrates from the Mediterranean still passes this village three times on three separate days.) She also raised high embankments on both sides of the Euphrates. In addition, she dug a vast lake above the city, a short distance from the river, deep enough to reach water and with a perimeter of some fifty-two miles. She used the excavated earth to raise the river embankments even higher. As the lake was dug, she had enormous stones brought to the edge. When all this was finished—the lake dug and the embankments built—she diverted the river into the new lake, filling it. While the old riverbed was empty, she accomplished two things: she lined both banks of the river through the city with baked brick, matching the riverside walls, and she built a bridge over the Euphrates from stones she had quarried for the lake, binding them together with iron and lead. During the day, square wooden platforms were laid across the stones for people to walk on. At night, the platforms were removed to prevent the inhabitants of the two halves of the city from crossing over and robbing each other. When the lake was full and the bridge finished, she turned the river back into its original course from the lake. The lake, now a marsh, served its purpose, and the citizens had a bridge.
